response:
READING

**The constraint that governs everything**

Idris Sankey-Marchmont's written report is the load-bearing fact in this analysis. It says, unambiguously, that rehousing and aqueous treatment carried out into the strongroom as it stands will need to be repeated within a decade. That is not a caution or a caveat — it is a professional determination that the GBP 250-per-item unit cost is not the real unit cost under LINDCASTER. The real unit cost is GBP 250 now plus GBP 250 again before roughly 2036, plus whatever inflation and re-mobilisation add to the second round. LINDCASTER's headline of 1,360 items treated has to be read as 1,360 items temporarily stabilised and then retreated. The comparison with HAVERSHOLT's 180 items is therefore false as stated.

**What the environment numbers mean**

62 per cent RH with an 11-point annual swing against a target of 45–55 per cent and a swing under 5: the strongroom is running at roughly 7–17 percentage points above the upper tolerance on absolute humidity and more than twice the permitted swing. That is not a marginal deviation. Acid hydrolysis in iron gall inks and the decay of acidic boards are both moisture-driven reactions; the conservator's decade warning flows directly from these numbers. Buffered enclosures holding a microclimate within 3 points of packing condition help with fluctuation but cannot correct a base RH of around 62 per cent. An item packed in a 62 per cent environment and held within 3 points of that is still at 59–65 per cent — above target throughout. The enclosures are a meaningful tool in a controlled environment; they are a moderating measure, not a substitute for one.

**The arithmetic of LINDCASTER over time**

1,360 items treated now: GBP 340,000
Plant in 2029–30 (GBP 295,000 in 2026 money; allow GBP 320,000–330,000 inflated): GBP 320,000–330,000 from the unallocated line
Re-treatment of the 1,360 items within the decade (now in a corrected environment, but still necessary per the conservator): a further GBP 340,000 at today's rates, more later
Remaining 1,540 at-risk items still untreated throughout

The cumulative spend to reach the same end-state as HAVERSHOLT under LINDCASTER is materially higher, and it requires two commitments that are not yet made: the 2029–30 board decision in November 2028 (nothing committed, competing claims possible, no guarantee the plant budget survives), and a second conservation contract thereafter. HAVERSHOLT requires one decision and one contract for each element.

**The 2029–30 capital line under each course**

Under HAVERSHOLT, the GBP 400,000 unallocated line in 2029–30 becomes a pure conservation budget. At GBP 250 per item it buys 1,600 items treated in a now-correct environment, durably. Combined with the 180 treated from the bequest that is 1,780 items — more than LINDCASTER's 1,360, and none of them needing retreatment. The board case for that allocation is straightforward: the environment is already fixed, the money goes directly to items, there is a clear project.

Under LINDCASTER, the board is being asked in November 2028 to fund the plant (which the bequest could have paid for), and the plant must come before conservation can resume durably. That is a harder case to make, the plant quote will need to be re-obtained (the Threlkeld quote expired January 2027), and the 2029–30 line may not stretch to both plant and meaningful conservation in the same programme.

**The rate of loss**

From 2019 to 2025 the unusable band grew from 640 to 1,010 items: approximately 62 items a year. That rate is measured in the existing environment. HAVERSHOLT does not eliminate deterioration before commissioning in May 2027 — roughly nine months from now, or about 47 more items into the unusable band — but it arrests the environmental contribution to degradation for all 4,200 from that point. LINDCASTER, treating at 70 items a month, reaches all 1,360 items over about 19–20 months (to approximately April 2028), during which time roughly 100 more items pass into the unusable band among the untreated 2,900 — and the 2,900 minus 1,360 = 1,540 items never reached by this bequest remain in the damaging environment indefinitely thereafter.

**The quote and order deadline**

The Threlkeld quote is held to 2027-01-30. The order must be placed fourteen weeks before the 2027-05-29 commissioning date, which works out to approximately 20 February 2027. The effective order deadline is therefore 30 January 2027 to secure the quoted price; that is about five months away and is achievable. Delaying the decision to explore LINDCASTER risks losing the price-hold and pushing commissioning past the bequest deadline or into a re-quote that will be higher.

**Weighing the courses directly**

The case for LINDCASTER rests on three propositions: (1) 1,360 items is a larger number than 180; (2) the enclosures will hold long enough; (3) the plant will come through the 2029–30 programme. All three are weakened by the conservator's report. Proposition (1) is undermined because the 1,360 items are not lastingly treated. Proposition (2) is partial at best in a 62 per cent RH environment. Proposition (3) is a board decision not yet made, requiring a new quote and competing for an unallocated line.

The case for HAVERSHOLT rests on: (1) the conservator's written professional judgment that environmental control is prerequisite to durable treatment; (2) the plant fixing the conditions for all 4,200 items, not 1,360; (3) the 2029–30 line being available for pure conservation thereafter; (4) no money being spent twice. All four hold.

The 180-item treatment figure looks small, and it is small. But treating 180 items that stay treated is a different proposition from treating 1,360 that need doing again. The right comparison is HAVERSHOLT now plus the 2029–30 programme (1,780 items durable) against LINDCASTER now plus 2029–30 plant plus 2030s retreatment (uncertain, expensive, delayed). HAVERSHOLT wins that comparison.

---

READING
  The core analytical question is whether the conservator's judgment — that treatment in the current environment must be repeated within a decade — is sufficient to reframe LINDCASTER's apparent advantage in item numbers. It is. Treating 1,360 items in an uncorrected strongroom is not equivalent to treating 1,360 items durably. The environmental plant is not an alternative to conservation spending; it is the precondition that makes conservation spending stick. HAVERSHOLT spends the bequest on fixing that precondition and begins treatment. LINDCASTER spends the bequest on treatment that the Institute's own conservator has said in writing will need to be done again. Additionally: the 2029–30 unallocated line is a better vehicle for conservation (which is fully discretionary and repeatable across years) than for plant (which has a hard technical specification and should be funded against a dedicated capital line — which the bequest provides). Deferring the plant to an uncommitted future board decision to free up money for treatment that will need repeating is the definition of false economy here. The timing of the Threlkeld quote (expiring January 2027) adds urgency but is not in itself decisive; the conservator's report is.

CALL
  HAVERSHOLT

GROUNDS
  The conservator's written finding that treatment in the uncorrected environment must be repeated within a decade means LINDCASTER's 1,360 items are not durably treated, so the apparent numerical advantage is illusory, and HAVERSHOLT's plant corrects the root condition for all 4,200 items while leaving the 2029–30 unallocated line free for lasting conservation work.
